extracted.intended_audience: professional journalists, U.N. delegates, and general news readers
extracted.subtask_description: Coverage of a U.N. subcommission proposal to call a world conference of professional newsmen to consider a universal code of ethics for journalists, including debate over its feasibility, proposed amendments, and procedural arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal code of ethics for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: U.N. subcommission voted to call a world conference of professional newsmen to consider a universal code of ethics for journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only six of the 12 experts voted for the conference; there was doubt whether the U.N. Assembly would finance it. If held, a special preparatory committee of five professional newsmen would be named by the Secretary-General to arrange the conference sometime before the end of 1953; the conference would base its discussions on a draft code being prepared by the subcommission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparatory committee and procedural requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A special preparatory committee of five professional newsmen would be named by Secretary-General Trygve Lie to arrange the conference and prepare for its proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resolution asked the 1952 U.N. Assembly to finance the project; the preparatory committee would work before the proposed 1953 conference and base discussions on the draft code prepared by the subcommission. Practical issues raised included funding and whether the Assembly would support the expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility given differing concepts of press function
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition argument (Carroll Binder) that it is futile to try to draft a universal code in the face of widely different concepts of the press functions in the Communist and free countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binder said many U.S. professional newspaper groups lack enthusiasm for the proposal; he also noted a large number of expected abstentions, which he took as indicating lack of support for a world conference or a single universal code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contention over ideological obligations in a code
rubrics_metrics.description: Soviet representative Vasily Zonov proposed amendments that would state it is the obligation of newsmen to fight against 'what the Russians call warmongers' and to oppose fascism and discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These amendments were rejected by the subcommission; the vote split and abstentions reflect disagreement over embedding explicit ideological duties in a universal code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for neutral, fact-finding investigation of wartime atrocity/epidemic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretary Acheson's proposal that the International Red Cross be allowed to investigate reports of epidemics and charges (e.g., of germ warfare) so that facts can be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such investigations require cooperation by both sides; the article notes the Communists had refused to let the Red Cross make investigations in some areas, and that neutral access and verification are prerequisites for credible reporting on such charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of press access and safe-conduct for war correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Press access to negotiation sites and battle areas (e.g., Kaesong) and permission for war correspondents to travel and report were discussed as part of truce/negotiation arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chronology recounts episodes where press access was barred or required safe-conduct guarantees; the practical criterion for reporting includes permitting free movement of personnel and a free choice of who should go, including correspondents, to ensure independent coverage.
